'''''Bryopsis''''', often referred to as '''hair algae''',<ref>{{cite book |last1=Goemans |first1=Bob |title=The 'Living' Marine Aquarium Manual Basic And Advanced Husbandry For The 'Modern' Marine Aquarium |date=2012 |publisher=Salt Corner |isbn=978-0-615-60306-3 |url=https://www.saltcorner.com/LMAM/ShowChapter.php?ChapterID=18 |access-date=29 August 2024 |chapter=12 – Algae: the Good, Bad, and Ugly}}</ref> is a [[genus]] of marine [[green algae]] in the family [[Bryopsidaceae]].<ref name="Algaebase"/> Species in the genus are macroscopic, siphonous marine green algae that are made up of units of single tubular filaments. They can form dense tufts up to 40 cm in height.<ref name="gio2018">{{cite journal | last1=Giovagnetti | first1=Vasco | last2=Han | first2=Guangye | last3=Ware | first3=Maxwell A. | last4=Ungerer | first4=Petra | last5=Qin | first5=Xiaochun | last6=Wang | first6=Wen-Da | last7=Kuang | first7=Tingyun | last8=Shen | first8=Jian-Ren | last9=Ruban | first9=Alexander V. | title=A siphonous morphology affects light-harvesting modulation in the intertidal green macroalga Bryopsis corticulans (Ulvophyceae) | journal=Planta | date=2018 | volume=247 | issue=6 | pages=1293–1306 | doi=10.1007/s00425-018-2854-5 | pmid=29460179 | pmc=5945744 }}</ref><ref name="fong2019">{{cite journal | last1=Fong | first1=Jenny | last2=Lim | first2=Zi Wei | last3=Bauman | first3=Andrew G. | last4=Valiyaveettil | first4=Suresh | last5=Liao | first5=Lawrence M. | last6=Yip | first6=Zhi Ting | last7=Todd | first7=Peter A. | title=Allelopathic effects of macroalgae on Pocillopora acuta coral larvae | journal=Marine Environmental Research | date=2019 | volume=151 | article-number=104745 | doi=10.1016/j.marenvres.2019.06.007 | pmid=31229278 }}</ref> Each cell is made of up an erect [[thallus]] that is often branched into pinnules.<ref name="green1960">{{cite journal | last1=Green | first1=Paul B. | title=Wall Structure and Lateral Formation in the Alga Bryopsis | journal=American Journal of Botany | date=1960 | volume=47 | issue=6 | pages=476–481 | doi=10.2307/2439562 | jstor=2439562 }}</ref> Approximately 60 species have been identified in this genus since its initial discovery in 1809.<ref name="jvlam1809">{{cite journal |last=Lamouroux |first=J. V. |year=1809 |title=Mémoire sur trois nouveaux genres de la famille des Algues marines: Dictyopteris, Amansia, Bryopsis |journal=Journal de Botanique |volume=2 |pages=129–135}}</ref>  The ecological success of ''Bryopsis'' has also been attributed to its associations with endophytic bacteria that reside in the [[cytoplasm]] of their cells.<ref name="hollelverwi2013">{{cite journal | last1=Hollants | first1=Joke | last2=Leliaert | first2=Frederik | last3=Verbruggen | first3=Heroen | last4=Willems | first4=Anne | last5=De Clerck | first5=Olivier | title=Permanent residents or temporary lodgers: Characterizing intracellular bacterial communities in the siphonous green alga ''Bryopsis'' | journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences | date=2013 | volume=280 | issue=1754 | doi=10.1098/rspb.2012.2659 | pmid=23303543 | pmc=3574326 }}</ref>

Species in this genus are known to be pests in aquariums and associated with green tides due to macroalgal blooms.<ref>{{cite web |title=Bryopsis pennata J.V.Lamouroux 1809 |url=http://www.hawaii.edu/reefalgae/invasive_algae/chloro/bryopsis_pennata.htm |work=Marine Algae of Hawai{{okina}}i}}</ref><ref name=song2019>{{cite journal | last1=Song | first1=Wei | last2=Wang | first2=Zongling | last3=Li | first3=Yan | last4=Han | first4=Hongbin | last5=Zhang | first5=Xuelei | title=Tracking the original source of the green tides in the Bohai Sea, China | journal=Estuarine, Coastal and Shelf Science | date=2019 | volume=219 | pages=354–362 | doi=10.1016/j.ecss.2019.02.036 }}</ref><ref name=han2020>{{cite journal | last1=Jiang | first1=Weiling | last2=Yu | first2=Xiaolei | last3=Zhang | first3=Huanyu | last4=Wang | first4=Yu | last5=Tian | first5=Xiaoxuan | title=The complete mitochondrial genome sequence of ''Aulacophora indica'' | journal=Mitochondrial DNA Part B | date=2020 | volume=5 | issue=1 | pages=184–185 | doi=10.1080/23802359.2019.1698378 | pmid=33366478 | pmc=7748638 }}</ref> However, ''Bryopsis'' also contains unique chemical properties, most notably, Kahalalide F (KF), a [[depsipeptide]] that is being studied for its antitumor properties in human cancer cells and also has important ecological significance in protecting the algae against herbivory. The removal of algal blooms for the extraction of KF may be a pragmatic approach to eradicating ''Bryopsis'' from green tides and aiding the economic burden of producing KF experimentally for clinical trials.

== Morphology and cell biology ==
[[File:Bryopsis vestita 29062289.jpg|thumb|''[[Bryopsis vestita]]'']]
''Bryopsis'' is a filamentous green alga that can forms dense tufts between 2 – 40 cm tall.<ref name="Algaebase" /><ref name="fong2019" /> It tends to have a morphology that is simple, non-calcified and siphonous multinucleate filaments with no cross walls, with axes that are erect and uniaxial. Its fronds are feather-like, extended with prostate axes.<ref name="Oliveira-2021">{{Cite journal |last1=Oliveira |first1=Marcella Guennes Tavares de |last2=Pereira |first2=Sonia Maria Barreto |last3=Benko-Iseppon |first3=Ana Maria |last4=Balbino |first4=Valdir Queiroz |last5=Silva Junior |first5=Wilson José da |last6=Ximenes |first6=Caroline Feijão |last7=Carvalho |first7=Maria de Fátima de Oliveira |last8=Cassano |first8=Valéria |date=2021-01-25 |title=First molecular analysis of the genus Bryopsis (Bryopsidales, Chlorophyta) from Brazil, with an emphasis on the Pernambuco coast |journal=Acta Botanica Brasilica |language=en |volume=35 |issue=2 |pages=161–178 |doi=10.1590/0102-33062020abb0154 |issn=0102-3306 |s2cid=234049944 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Morabito-2010">{{Cite journal |last1=Morabito |first1=Marina |last2=Gargiulo |first2=Gaetano |last3=Genovese |first3=Giusi |year=2010 |title=A review of life history pathways in Bryopsis |journal=Atti dell’Accademia Peloritana dei Pericolanti. Classe di Scienze Fisiche, Matematiche e Naturali|volume=88 |issue=2 |doi=10.1478/C1A1002005}}</ref> Organisms are single tubular cells that are siphonous, which is a term used to describe algae in which the thallus is not compartmentalized and typically contains a large vacuole surrounded by an outer later of protoplasm. The nuclei and chloroplasts reside in the thallus and line the cell wall. When extruded, the protoplasm can survive without a cell membrane for several minutes before regenerating into mature individual units.<ref name="lu2011">{{cite journal | last1=Lü | first1=Fang | last2=Xü | first2=Wei | last3=Tian | first3=Chao | last4=Wang | first4=Guangce | last5=Niu | first5=Jiangfeng | last6=Pan | first6=Guanghua | last7=Hu | first7=Songnian | title=The Bryopsis hypnoides Plastid Genome: Multimeric Forms and Complete Nucleotide Sequence | journal=PLOS ONE | date=2011 | volume=6 | issue=2 | article-number=e14663 | doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0014663 | pmid=21339817 | doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="holldeclel2011">{{cite journal | last1=Hollants | first1=Joke | last2=Decleyre | first2=Helen | last3=Leliaert | first3=Frederik | last4=De Clerck | first4=Olivier | last5=Willems | first5=Anne | title=Life without a cell membrane: Challenging the specificity of bacterial endophytes within Bryopsis (Bryopsidales, Chlorophyta) | journal=BMC Microbiology | date=2011 | volume=11 | page=255 | doi=10.1186/1471-2180-11-255 | pmid=22103477 | pmc=3252328 | doi-access=free }}</ref> The thallus is commonly erect and occurs in two morphologies corresponding to haploid or diploid life cycle stages: the macrothallus and microthallus.<ref name="hollelverwi2013" /> The growth of the macrothallus is indeterminate, while the microthallus is often determinate.<ref name="Algaebase" /> The fronds of Bryopsis vary among species from deltoid to lanceolate and the pinnules are most commonly in radial, distichous or secund arrangements.<ref name="krell2001">{{Cite journal |last1=Krellwitz |first1=Erin C. |last2=Kowallik |first2=Klaus V. |last3=Manos |first3=Paul S. |date=2001-07-01 |title=Molecular and morphological analyses of Bryopsis (Bryopsidales, Chlorophyta) from the western North Atlantic and Caribbean |journal=Phycologia |volume=40 |issue=4 |pages=330–339 |doi=10.2216/i0031-8884-40-4-330.1 |issn=0031-8884 |s2cid=85400815}}</ref>

Previous research on the morphology of this genus has correlated the wall structure with the cell shape of Bryopsis. The cell walls are tough yet flexible.<ref name="gio2018" /> The main components of the cell wall are mannan, cellulose and xylan.<ref name="huizing1975">{{cite journal | last1=Huizing | first1=H.J. | last2=Rietema | first2=H. | title=Xylan and mannan as cell wall constituents of different stages in the life-histories of some siphoneous green algae | journal=British Phycological Journal | date=1975 | volume=10 | pages=13–16 | doi=10.1080/00071617500650021 }}</ref><ref name="Brück">{{cite journal | last1=Brück | first1=B. | last2=Schnetter | first2=R. | title=Life history and karyology of Bryopsis plumosa (Chlorophyta, Bryopsidales) from the Canary Islands | journal=Phycologia | date=1997 | volume=36 | issue=2 | pages=128–137 | doi=10.2216/i0031-8884-36-2-128.1 }}</ref> Its meristematic activity is conveniently differentiated from the typical mechanism in that it is free of cross-walls, is not covered by mature laterals and its laterals all lie in the same plane, so new mass is added to the inner surface of the growing walls from transverse microfibrils.<ref name="green1960" /> The apical development and arrangement of transverse microfibrils play an important role in the lateral and longitudinal growth of the cell wall structure.<ref name="green1960" />

The chloroplast is the largest organelle in the cell of ''Bryopsis''.<ref name="lu2011" /> Its relative vitality compared to other organelles in unfavourable conditions and its ability to photosynthesize and lodge in other cells demonstrates its high level of autonomy relative to other organelles.<ref name="lu2011" /> The chloroplast is also thought to have an important role in protoplast regeneration. The literature suggests that the fast rate of repair to photosystem II and transient photoinactivation are mechanisms that this genus uses to help mitigate photodamage from excess sun light.<ref name="gio2018" /> The siphonous morphology of ''Bryopsis'' also plays an important role in adapting to changing light conditions on the intertidal shores; affecting light-harvesting modulation in some species of this genus.<ref name="gio2018" /> Some species of ''Bryopsis'' have a protective state in which their bodies discriminate between surface filaments that get high exposure to the sun from those that reside in underlayers.

''Bryopsis'' is a unicellular coenocytic cell.<ref name="lu2011" /> In the macrothallus, nuclei are approximately 25 μm in diameter, while in the microthallus the primary nucleus can be up to 60 μm.<ref name="minami2005">{{cite journal | last1=Minamikawa | first1=Bunji | last2=Yamagishi | first2=Takahiro | last3=Hishinuma | first3=Tasuku | last4=Ogawa | first4=Shigeru | title=Behavior of nuclei during zoosporogenesis in Bryopsis plumosa (Bryopsidales, Chlorophyta) | journal=Journal of Plant Research | date=2005 | volume=118 | issue=1 | pages=43–48 | doi=10.1007/s10265-005-0193-7 | pmid=15700111 }}</ref><ref name="Brück" /> The nucleolus of the primary nucleus is spherical and around 20 μm in diameter. In many species of this genus, it has been observed that nuclear volume is not related to nuclear DNA content.<ref name="Brück" /> In the sporophyte stage, the nucleus is 10 μm diameter. Once the nucleus of the sporophyte reaches a sufficient size, it will start to divide, resulting in a multinucleated sporophyte. This arrangement is aided by centrioles which help to separate the chromosomes and split the nucleus into two daughter nuclei. After the first division, the nucleus of the sporophyte is the same size the nuclei in the mature macrothallus.<ref name="Brück" /> The subsequent division of the cytoplasm results in uninucleate masses of [[protoplasm]].

==Life cycle==
The life history patterns of ''Bryopsis'' are highly variable, potentially the most diverse among any genus of green algae.<ref name="Morabito-2010" /> ''Bryopsis'' have highly variable life history patterns, even within species. The life cycle of ''Bryopsis'' has two stages alternating between an erect macroscopic stage which form macrothalli and a small branched phase which form microthalli.<ref name="Brück" /> Macrothalli are haploid while microthalli are diploid.<ref name="Morabito-2010" /> Haploid macrothalli may either produce gametes that will then fuse to make a zygote and then a sporophyte (microthallus), or they may produce microthalli at the tips of fronds whose cytoplasms are always kept separate from that of the "mother" organism, the macrothallus. In this specialized region, diploid and haploid nuclei can both be found, but the exact mechanism of diploidization is poorly understood.<ref name="Brück" /> This means that in Bryopsis diploidization to produce microthalli is not dependent on syngamy, it can happen within the macrothallus. This can be disadvantageous due to the loss of genetic exchange, but it is advantageous because the direct development of microthalli does not depend on mating so new microthalli can be produced relatively quickly. Microthalli formed in this way then detach from the gametophyte to form separate sporophytes. Macrothalli develop either directly from microthalli, or through [[stephanokont]]ic zoospores which form from them.<ref name="minami2005" />

Stephanokontic zoospores are flagellated cells that develop into gametophytes upon attachment to substrate.<ref name="minami2005" /> Stephanokontic zoospores in the life cycles of ''Bryopsis'' have been observed in many species. However, some species within Bryopsis do not have stephanokonic zoospores and produce macrothalli directly from microthalli. Both methods of development can occur within one species, as observed in B. plumosa.<ref name="minami2005" /> The timing of meiosis in ''Bryopsis'' is not well understood.

''[[In vitro]] c''ultivation of ''Bryopsis hypnoides'' has revealed new information that is important in its regeneration. In environments where conditions are suboptimal, organelle aggregation among ''B. hypnoides'' was found to be a possible response to survive.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Guang-Ce |last2=Tseng |first2=Cheng-Kui |date=2006 |title=Culturing the Segments of Bryopsis hypnoides Lamouroux Thalli Regenerated from Protoplast Aggregations |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1744-7909.2006.00190.x |journal=Journal of Integrative Plant Biology |language=en |volume=48 |issue=2 |pages=190–196 |doi=10.1111/j.1744-7909.2006.00190.x |issn=1744-7909|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Distribution== 
[[File:Bryopsis cf. pennata Réunion.jpg|thumb|''Bryopsis'' [[cf.]] ''pennata'' at [[Réunion]]]]
''Bryopsis'' contains mostly epilithic but sometimes free-floating algae that occupy a range of habitats including seaweed beds, shallow fringing reefs and both sheltered and well-exposed subtidal areas.<ref name="song2019" /><ref name="gio2018" /> ''Bryopsis'' is widely distributed in tropical and subtropical areas and dominant in eutrophic coastal regions.<ref name="hollelverwi2013" /> ''B. pennata'', ''B. hyponoides'' and ''B. plumosa'' are among the most common cosmopolitan species within this genus.<ref name="krell2001" /> In addition to having a wide distribution, this genus can have a high species density. For example, in Singapore it represents one of the four functional-form groups that makes up approximately 20-40% of benthic cover across coral reefs<ref name="fong2019" /> and along the east coast of the United States and the Caribbean, where clusters of species from this genus dominate intertidal regions.<ref name="krell2001" /> A majority of the species tend to inhabit marine ecosystems with temperatures that range from 5 to 27 degrees celsius, among coral reefs and near the shore, associated to rocky substrates however, some may also inhabit mangrove areas, estuaries, and other brackish systems.<ref name="Oliveira-2021" />

''Bryopsis'' is widely distributed along tropical, subtropical, and temperate coastal regions and thrives in eutrophic waters.<ref name="krell2001" /> ''Bryopsis'' can be epilithic or free-floating. Climate warming and pollution are factors that are thought to contribute to its increased presence over the past few years.<ref name="song2019" /> The genus is also widely distributed in Brazil, with studies spanning from the late 1800 to 2015.<ref name="Oliveira-2021" />

==Ecology==
''Bryopsis'' are regarded to have ecological significance as primary producers, also as refuge for other marine organisms.<ref name="Oliveira-2021" /> It may also be possible that some species within the genus are invasive in nature, seeing how it thrives in eutrophic conditions. They may function as bioindicators.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Williams |first1=Susan L. |last2=Smith |first2=Jennifer E. |date=2007-12-01 |title=A Global Review of the Distribution, Taxonomy, and Impacts of Introduced Seaweeds |url=https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/10.1146/annurev.ecolsys.38.091206.095543 |journal=Annual Review of Ecology, Evolution, and Systematics |language=en |volume=38 |issue=1 |pages=327–359 |doi=10.1146/annurev.ecolsys.38.091206.095543 |issn=1543-592X|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== Herbivory ===
For benthic organisms like ''Bryopsis'', herbivory is an important factor influencing species density and mortality. Chemically mediated predator-prey interactions such as the production of kahalalide F (KF), helps protect ''Bryopsis'' from herbivory. However, [[Sacoglossa]]ns are an exception, they are a type of opisthobranch mollusk that eat siphonaceous green algae.<ref name="becerro2001">{{cite journal | last1=Becerro | first1=Mikel A. | last2=Goetz | first2=Gilles | last3=Paul | first3=Valerie J.|author3-link=Valerie Paul | last4=Scheuer | first4=Paul J. | title=Chemical Defenses of the Sacoglossan Mollusk Elysia rufescens and Its Host Alga Bryopsis sp | journal=Journal of Chemical Ecology | date=2001 | volume=27 | issue=11 | pages=2287–2299 | doi=10.1023/A:1012287105923 | pmid=11817082 }}</ref> They are highly specialized herbivores that sequester chloroplasts and other secondary metabolites from their diet has a source of photosynthetic energy.<ref name="becerro2001" /> The literature has demonstrated that both ''Bryopsis'' and the mollusks that feed on it are protected from fish predation due to the presence of KF. The sequestration of secondary metabolites such as KF provides the mollusks a diet-derived chemical defense against predation. Therefore, ''Bryopsis'' has an influential role on the ecology and evolution of mollusk species that feed on it.

=== Competitive interactions with coral reefs ===
Globally, coral reef ecosystems are degrading due to anthropogenic effects such as pollution and climate change.<ref name="haas2014">{{cite journal | last1=Haas | first1=Andreas F. | last2=Smith | first2=Jennifer E. | last3=Thompson | first3=Melissa | last4=Deheyn | first4=Dimitri D. | title=Effects of reduced dissolved oxygen concentrations on physiology and fluorescence of hermatypic corals and benthic algae | journal=PeerJ | date=2014 | volume=2 | article-number=e235 | doi=10.7717/peerj.235 | pmid=24482757 | pmc=3898309 | doi-access=free }}</ref> The proliferation of ''Bryopsis'' has also influenced the dramatic decline in coral reefs by limiting survivorship and potentially constrain recovery of degrading reefs.<ref name="fong2019" /> The larvae of coral are vulnerable to competition with macroalgae. ''Bryopsis'' reduces survivorship of coral larvae through allelopathic effects, occupying large amounts of geographical space, and destabilizing coral microbiomes. Increasing concentrations of allelochemicals produced by ''Bryopsis'' results in increased larval mortality rates. These effects extend beyond the duration of chemical exposure because even when no traces remained, the mortality rate of coral larvae continued to increase in experimental conditions.<ref name="fong2019" />

Hypoxia may be another factor that contributes to the competitive interactions between coral and macroalgae. Bryopsis is tolerant to low oxygen concentration environments that were detrimental to coral species.<ref name="haas2014" /> Additionally, the coral skeleton that remains after tissue degradation optimizes colonization by microalgae, which attach to the exposed hard substrate.<ref name="haas2014" /> Therefore, the recovery of degrading coral reefs containing macroalgae may be negatively affected due to ''Bryopsis''{{'}} wider range of tolerance for suboptimal conditions and its allelopathic effects on the survivorship and settlement of coral larvae.

=== Green tides ===
[[Algal bloom]]s occur in various coastal regions worldwide. ''Bryopsis'' is one of the main genera of macroalgae contributing to this. Microbes break down the macroalgae that accumulate in the ocean and intertidal regions. The decomposition of algae causes oxygen shortages and hypoxic or anoxic, lethal environments for other organisms.<ref name="song2019" /> This could have serious effects on the ecosystem. Rising sea water temperatures and eutrophication are thought to be major factors responsible for the development of green tides. ''Bryopsis'' micro-propagules in the form of gametes, spores and zygotes attach to existing mature thalli or seaweed beds and this initiates the green tides. Algal blooms could have significant ecological repercussions if they are not contained due to their potentially harmful effects on other organisms.

=== Bacterial associations ===
Bacterial associations with marine macroalgae are common. They are often found on the surface and in the cytoplasm or vacuoles of the cells and can influence the life cycle as well as different metabolic functions such as growth factors, and the fixation of nitrogen and antimicrobial compounds of the macroalgae.<ref name="hollelverwi2013" /> Bacteria-like particles have been identified in the cytoplasm of the thalli and gametes of ''Bryopsis''. The latter supports the theory of vertical transmission of endophytic bacteria, implying a stable and mutualistic relationship between the host and its [[endobiont]]s.<ref name="holller2011">{{cite journal | last1=Hollants | first1=Joke | last2=Leroux | first2=Olivier | last3=Leliaert | first3=Frederik | last4=Decleyre | first4=Helen | last5=De Clerck | first5=Olivier | last6=Willems | first6=Anne | title=Who is in There? Exploration of Endophytic Bacteria within the Siphonous Green Seaweed Bryopsis (Bryopsidales, Chlorophyta) | journal=PLOS ONE | date=2011 | volume=6 | issue=10 | article-number=e26458 | doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0026458 | pmid=22028882 | pmc=3196581 | doi-access=free }}</ref> Bryopsis is thought to have intrinsic mechanisms that are highly selective for specific bacteria despite being exposed to a wide range of marine bacteria.<ref name="holldeclel2011" /> The functionality of the presence of these endosymbionts is not well known however, they are thought to provide the algae an adaptive advantage.<ref name="hollelverde2013">{{cite journal | last1=Hollants | first1=Joke | last2=Leliaert | first2=Frederik | last3=Verbruggen | first3=Heroen | last4=De Clerck | first4=Olivier | last5=Willems | first5=Anne | title=Host specificity and coevolution of Flavobacteriaceae endosymbionts within the siphonous green seaweed Bryopsis | journal=Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution | date=2013 | volume=67 | issue=3 | pages=608–614 | doi=10.1016/j.ympev.2013.02.025 | pmid=23499613 }}</ref> A strong host specific association between Flavobacteriaceae endosymbionts and ''Bryopsis'' has been cited in literature to aid nitrogen fixation in the algae.<ref name="hollelverde2013" /> Generalist phylotypes fulfill metabolic functions such as nitrogen-fixation ([[Rhizobiaceae]]), anoxygenic photosynthesis ([[Phyllobacteriaceae]]) and CO-oxidation (''[[Labrenzia]]'').<ref name="hollelverwi2013" />

== Human interactions ==

=== Clinical applications ===
''Bryopsis'' is a source of bioactive compounds such as therapeutic [[kahalalide]]s.<ref name="holller2011" /> Kahalalide F (KF) acts against human cancer cell lines.<ref name="wang2015">{{cite journal | last1=Wang | first1=Bin | last2=Waters | first2=Amanda L. | last3=Valeriote | first3=Frederick A. | last4=Hamann | first4=Mark T. | title=An efficient and cost-effective approach to kahalalide F N-terminal modifications using a nuisance algal bloom of Bryopsis pennata | journal=Biochimica et Biophysica Acta (BBA) - General Subjects | date=2015 | volume=1850 | issue=9 | pages=1849–1854 | doi=10.1016/j.bbagen.2015.05.004 | pmid=25964068 | pmc=4516563 }}</ref><ref name="becerro2001" /> Clinical trials have demonstrated that when KF is combined with its other isomers it is highly sensitive to drug resistant strains of cancer.<ref name="Suárez2003">{{cite journal | last1=Suárez | first1=Y. | last2=González | first2=L. | last3=Cuadrado | first3=A. | last4=Berciano | first4=M. | last5=Lafarga | first5=M. | last6=Muñoz | first6=A. | title=Kahalalide F, a new marine-derived compound, induces oncosis in human prostate and breast cancer cells | journal=Molecular Cancer Therapeutics | date=2003 | volume=2 | issue=9 | pages=863–872 | pmid=14555705 }}</ref> The potential for clinical application is being explored, though the mechanism by which KF targets cancer cells is not well understood. Potentially invasive green algae that grow as a result of algal blooms could be recovered to extract KF for clinical purposes.<ref name="Suárez2003" /> This is thought to be a pragmatic approach to addressing the ecological impact of green macroalgae blooms and the economic burden associated with manufacturing KF for clinical trials.

Bioactive compounds are also known to be present among ''Bryopsis,'' specifically among ''B. pennata'' and ''B. plumosa'' with different biological activities such as antifungal, antibacterial, and anticoagulant properties.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Ibrahim |first1=Muhammad |chapter=Chapter 6 - Algae-Based Biologically Active Compounds |date=2017-01-01 |title=Algae Based Polymers, Blends, and Composites |pages=155–271 |editor-last=Zia |editor-first=Khalid Mahmood |chapter-url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780128123607000069 |access-date=2022-01-24 |publisher=Elsevier |editor2-last=Zuber |editor2-first=Mohammad |editor3-last=Ali |editor3-first=Muhammad}}</ref> Bioactive compounds found in the genus are also being used as treatments for different types of cancers === Aquaria ===
[[File:Bryopsis.jpg|thumb|''Bryopsis'' in a [[reef aquarium]]]]
Species of ''Bryopsis'' commonly populate commercial aquariums. They are introduced to aquariums on [[live rock]]s and the nutrient rich environment is favorable for its growth.<ref name="manoa2001">{{cite web |url=https://www.hawaii.edu/reefalgae/invasive_algae/pdf%20files/bryopsis_pennata.pdf |publisher=U. of H. at. Manoa |year=2001 |title=Bryopsis pennata |work=Algae: Invasive Native |page=A-26}}</ref> With little competition or predation in these environments, ''Bryopsis'' can overtake the benthic surface creating unfavorable low-oxygen environments for other species.<ref name="manoa2001" /> The elimination and control of ''Bryopsis'' within aquariums is challenging to manage and has economic significance.

This algae is usually seen as a nuisance though it may be desirable in [[macroalgae]] tanks. Though it is rarely sold on its own, its coarse composition aids in accumulating [[detritus]] from which it can derive nutrients. Eradication can be achieved through the use of grazers (including several [[crabs]], [[mollusks]], and [[sea urchins]]), manual removal, light starvation, and nutrient reduction. Elevated [[magnesium]] may hinder the growth of the algae but can be dangerous to [[invertebrates]].<ref>Bryopsis ''[https://www.livealgae.co.uk/identification-of-nuisance-micro-algae-in-the-marine-aquarium/bryopsis-nuisance-algae]''. In: Livealgae UK [https://www.livealgae.co.uk/]</ref><ref>Bryopsis ''[https://www.melevsreef.com/critter/bryopsis]''. In: Melev's Reef [https://www.melevsreef.com]</ref><ref name="pest">Nuisance Algae ID Guide ''[https://www.reefcleaners.org/nuisance-algae-id-guide]''. In: Reef Cleaners [https://www.reefcleaners.org/]</ref>

''[[Bryopsis plumosa]]'' and ''[[Bryopsis pennata]]'' are especially troublesome.<ref name=pest />

==Discovery== 
[[Jean Vincent Félix Lamouroux|Jean Vincent Felix Lamouroux]] was the first person to differentiate green, red and brown algae. In 1809, he discovered five new marine algal genera and he cited his findings in the Journal de Botanique. Among them were the first five species in the genus ''Bryopsis'' (''B. pennata'', ''B. hypnoides'', ''B. arbuscula'', ''B. cupressina'' and ''B. muscosa'').<ref name="jvlam1809" /> He described this genus as being green, with feather-like fronds.<ref name="mlam1809">Lamouroux, M. (1809). Observations sur la physiologie des algues marines, et description de cinq nouveaux genres de cette famille. Nouveau Bulletin des Sciences, (6), 330–333. Retrieved from http://img.algaebase.org/pdf/562869E513ae231FB6qNk39FBB26/15755.pdf</ref> Lamouroux differentiated these species by their size, arrangement and densities of pinnules on the main axes of the thallus.<ref name="krell2001" />

In 1823, [[Jean-Baptiste Bory de Saint-Vincent|Bory de Saint Vincent]] brought forth the family of green algae Bryopsidaceae which included the genus ''Bryopsis'', (Bryopsidales, Ulvophyceae and Chlorophyta).<ref name="woolcott">{{cite journal | last1=Woolcott | first1=Geoffrey W. | last2=Knöller | first2=Kristin | last3=King | first3=Robert J. | title=Phylogeny of the Bryopsidaceae (Bryopsidales, Chlorophyta): Cladistic analyses of morphological and molecular data | journal=Phycologia | date=2000 | volume=39 | issue=6 | pages=471–481 | doi=10.2216/i0031-8884-39-6-471.1 }}</ref> Later, 4 other genera (''[[Bryopsidella]]'', ''[[Derbesia]]'', ''[[Pedobesia]]'' and ''[[Trichosolen]]'') were also placed in this family. Since Lamouroux's initial discovery, there have been over 60 ''Bryopsis'' species described worldwide.<ref name="krell2001" />

The discovery of the variety of life history patterns has been formative in understanding the relationship between ''Bryopsis'' and other genera in the order. The life history varies between species of ''Bryopsis'' and even within single species of this genus. The differentiation of new genera, such as ''Bryopsidella'', which was previously reported as ''Bryposis halymeniae'' and ''Derbesia neglecta'', resulted from the identification of its unique life history. This resulted in taxonomic reorganization at the family level.<ref name="Morabito-2010" />
Continuous morphological variations and their inherently simple thallus structure has made it difficult to differentiate species within this genus.<ref name="krell2001" /> Therefore, the use of molecular datasets is an important tool in differentiating species. Currently, research using the chloroplast genome of ''Bryopsis'' as an identifier for species level studies is being done. The entire chloroplast genome of ''B. plumosa'', ''B. maxima'' and ''B. hypnoides'' has been sequenced.<ref name="lu2011" /><ref name="krell2001" />

==Taxonomy and nomenclature== 
The word ''Bryopsis'' comes from Greek origins. ''Bry-'' comes from the Greek words ''bryos'' and ''byron'', meaning moss, blossom and bloom. ''Ópsis''  or ''Ypsis'' is the Greek word for appearance or sight.<ref name="mlam1809" /> ''-opsis'' is synonymous to "likeness" and used in naming living organisms with organic structures that resemble other pre-existing structures that have already been named.

''Bryopsis'' was originally described by Lamouroux in 1809, providing information on five species based on morphological appearance, specifically the pinnules, its number, lengths, and arrangement. In eastern USA, three species of ''Bryopsis'' namely: ''B. pennata'', ''B. hynoides, B. plumosa'' are known to inhabit together or separately.<ref name="krell2001" />

Challenges in identifying ''Bryopsis'' species often arise from the great number of categories between species within the genus due to phenotypic traits that are quite similar from one another. Morphological analysis alone can lead to misidentification of species and misuse of nomenclature. In order to fully understand the diversity within the genus, different physiological aspects have been analyzed (e.g. life cycle, chromosomes) however, these have been insufficient in further elucidating taxonomic issues within species. Thus, the need for research using genetic markers may be of primary importance in recognizing several species that are morphologically plastic in nature.<ref name="Oliveira-2021" />
